---
id: c-type-sizes
title: Overflow-Safe Sum
difficulty: Easy
order: 1
tags: long long, overflow, types
---
## Statement
Read `n` (1 ≤ n ≤ 2·10^5) and then `n` integers, each between −10^9 and 10^9. Print their sum, the minimum, the maximum and the mean with exactly 2 decimals.

The sum can reach 2·10^14, far beyond `int`. Choose types accordingly.

## Starter
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    int n;
    scanf("%d", &n);

    return 0;
}
```

## Hints
- Use `long long sum` and read the values as `int`, or `long long` with `%lld`.
- The mean is `(double)sum / n`.

## Solution
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    int n;
    scanf("%d", &n);
    long long sum = 0;
    int mn = 0, mx = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        int x;
        scanf("%d", &x);
        sum += x;
        if (i == 0 || x < mn) mn = x;
        if (i == 0 || x > mx) mx = x;
    }
    printf("%lld %d %d %.2f\n", sum, mn, mx, (double)sum / n);
    return 0;
}
```

With `int sum`, two values of 10^9 already overflow (2·10^9 > 2^31 − 1). That's signed overflow, which is undefined behaviour. Initialising `mn`/`mx` from the first element (`i == 0`) avoids guessing sentinel values. `INT_MAX`/`INT_MIN` from `<limits.h>` are the alternative.
